q: What is Figure A, a type of metal sheet that has a pattern of holes or slots punched into it, often used for filtering, ventilation, and decorative purposes?
n: Figure A is perforated metal sheet: holes or slots punched in a pattern, used for ventilation, filtering and decoration. Source: Industrial Perforators Association; Ching.

q: What is Figure B, a metal sheet that has been slits and stretched to form a mesh pattern, often used in security applications or as a surface material for strength and drainage?
n: Figure B is expanded metal sheet, slit and stretched into a diamond mesh, used for security, grating and drainage. Source: EMMA (Expanded Metal Manufacturers Association).

q: What is Figure C, a metal sheet with a raised diamond pattern, commonly used for flooring, stair treads, and traction surfaces?
n: Figure C is checkered (tread) plate, with a raised diamond pattern for slip-resistant floors and stair treads. Source: ASTM A786.

q: What is Figure D, a type of metal sheet with a series of parallel ridges or grooves, often used in roofing, siding, and construction for its strength and lightweight properties?
n: Figure D is corrugated metal sheet, with parallel ridges that add stiffness, used for roofing and siding. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is Figure E, a continuous roll of metal sheet that is wound into a coil, typically used for manufacturing, forming, and processing into other shapes or products?
n: Figure E is a metal sheet coil, a continuous rolled sheet processed into other products. Source: Steel industry terminology (ASTM A653).

q: Which item is the steel rafter?
n: A points to the sloping member of the rigid frame, the steel rafter. Source: Metal Building Manufacturers Association (MBMA) terminology.

q: Which item is the eave purlin?
n: Figure A marks the eave purlin (eave strut) at the junction of roof and wall. Source: MBMA, Metal Building Systems Manual.

q: Which item is the anchor bolt?
n: Figure D marks the anchor bolt fixing the frame base to the foundation. Source: MBMA; AISC Design Guide 1.

q: Which item is the corner post?
n: Figure C marks the corner post (corner column) of the end wall. Source: MBMA, Metal Building Systems Manual.

q: Which item is the post-and-beam end frame?
n: Figure B marks the post-and-beam end frame, the end-wall framing of the building. Source: MBMA, Metal Building Systems Manual.

q: What is Figure A, a type of wire used to securely bind reinforcement bars in concrete construction?
n: Figure A is tie wire (G.I. wire #16), used to bind rebar at intersections. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (tie wire).

q: What is Figure B, a type of wire used for security fencing, characterized by sharp edges or points along the wire?
n: Figure B is barbed wire, with sharp barbs along its strands, used for security fencing. Source: ASTM A121.

q: What is Figure C, a type of wire mesh made by welding the intersections of horizontal and vertical wires?
n: Figure C is welded wire (mesh), with wires welded at their intersections. Welded wire mesh is used as slab and wall reinforcement and for fencing and screens. Source: ASTM A1064.

q: What is Figure D, amesh made from metal wires that are woven or welded together to form a grid structure?
n: Figure D is wire mesh, metal wires woven or welded into a grid. Wire mesh is used for screens, fencing, plaster lath and light reinforcement. Source: ASTM E2016.

q: What is Figure E, a type of fencing material made from interwoven metal wire, commonly used for security and boundary purposes?
n: Figure E is cyclone wire (chain-link), woven wire fencing used for security and boundaries. Source: ASTM A392.

q: Which type of building benefits the most from steel construction?
n: Sports facilities need long column-free spans, where steel's high strength-to-weight ratio pays off most. Source: AISC; Schodek, Structures.

q: What is the main disadvantage of steel as a building material?
n: Steel's main drawback is corrosion. It needs protective coatings, and it also needs fireproofing. Source: AISC; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: When specifying fireproofing for steel, which material is the most expensive?
n: Encasing steel in poured concrete is the heaviest and most labour-intensive fireproofing, so it is the most expensive. Source: AISC Design Guide 19 (Fire Resistance of Structural Steel Framing).

q: Which of the following is a major steel construction company in the Philippines?
n: SteelAsia Manufacturing Corporation is the Philippines' largest steel bar and section maker. Source: SteelAsia (official site).

q: Who is mainly responsible for the structural design of steel members?
n: The civil/structural engineer of record is responsible for the structural design of steel members. Source: RA 544 (Civil Engineering Law); NSCP 2015.

q: What does W4 × 13 mean?
o: Steel flange weighing 4 lb, 13 in. high
Wide flange about 4 in. deep weighing 13 lb/ft
n: W4 × 13 is a wide-flange section with a nominal depth of 4 in, weighing 13 lb/ft. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual.

q: What do you call an I-beam used specifically as a steel column?
n: An H-shaped wide-flange section rolled for column use is called a universal column (UC, British usage). Source: BS 4-1 (structural steel sections).

q: Which part of an I-beam resists shear?
n: The web of an I-beam resists shear. The web connects the flanges and carries most of the vertical shear force. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual; Gere & Goodno.

q: An I-shape with equal or nearly equal width and depth best suits use as a:
n: An I-shape with nearly equal width and depth (an H or column section) best suits columns, with good buckling resistance about both axes. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual.

q: What is the central vertical plate of a wide flange section?
n: The web is the central vertical plate of a wide-flange section. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual.

q: An I-beam is also known as a:
n: A standard I-beam is also called a universal beam (UB, British usage). Source: BS 4-1; AISC terminology.

q: Which is NOT a standard steel section abbreviation?
n: SHS, CHS and RHS are square, circular and rectangular hollow sections. "HHS" is not a standard abbreviation. Source: BS EN 10210; AISC.

q: What is an I-beam mainly used as?
n: An I-beam is shaped for bending, so it is used mainly as a beam. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual.

q: What is the typical use of a wide flange section?
n: Wide-flange (W/H) sections with near-equal flange widths are typically used as columns. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual.

q: What are the horizontal plates of a wide flange beam called?
n: The horizontal plates of a wide-flange beam are the flanges. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual.

q: Which part of an I-beam carries most of the bending?
n: The flanges, farthest from the neutral axis, carry most of the bending stress. Source: Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials.

q: What does the web of an I-beam do?
n: The web of an I-beam mainly resists shear. The flanges carry most of the bending stress, leaving the web to take shear. Source: Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials.

q: Which section suits long-span uses like bridges?
n: I-beams and W-sections, with high bending capacity, suit long-span uses like bridges. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual.

q: What is the main advantage of wide flange sections?
o: High moment of inertia and bending capacity
n: Wide-flange sections are efficient in bending because their material sits in the flanges, giving a high moment of inertia. Source: Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials.

q: Who is a local manufacturer of prestressed bars?
n: Benedicto Steel Group is a local manufacturer of steel bars, including prestressing bars. Source: Benedicto Steel Group (company site).

q: What is the name of the popular local supplier of structural steel in the Philippines?
n: SteelAsia is the popular local supplier of structural steel (rebar and sections) in the Philippines. Source: SteelAsia (official site).
